relearning.title: Read: isotopes and isotope notation
relearning.description: A short reading with the backpack analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can explain what isotopes are and use isotope notation to describe them.**

**Think of two backpacks of the same model.** Same brand, same color, same name tag. One has 2 textbooks inside and the other has 4. One is heavier, but it is still the same backpack with the same name tag. In isotopes, the **protons** are the name tag (they give the atom its identity), and the **neutrons** are the extra books (they add mass but don't change what the atom is).

**Isotopes** are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
**Same:** the number of protons, the atomic number, and (in a neutral atom) the number of electrons. Same electrons means isotopes react the same way.
**Different:** the number of neutrons, so the **mass number** (protons + neutrons) is different too.

**Hyphen notation** is the element name, a dash and the mass number: potassium-40, or C-12. To count: p⁺ = atomic number, n⁰ = mass number − atomic number, and e⁻ = p⁺ in a neutral atom.

**Worked example:** Are carbon-12 and carbon-14 isotopes? Both are carbon, atomic number 6, so both have 6 protons. Neutrons: 12 − 6 = 6 and 14 − 6 = 8. Same protons, different neutrons, so **yes, they are isotopes of carbon.**

checks.prompt: Two isotopes of the same element always have the same number of:
checks.explanation: Isotopes share the same protons (the name tag) and differ in neutrons. If the protons changed, it would be a different element. Thinking isotopes have different protons is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Nitrogen has atomic number 7. How many neutrons are in nitrogen-15? Type a number.
checks.explanation: The number after the dash is the mass number, 15. n⁰ = 15 − 7 = 8. Reading the 15 as the number of neutrons is the common mistake.

sections.title: Nuclear notation and average atomic mass

body.text:
**Nuclear notation** puts the mass number on top and the atomic number on the bottom, to the left of the symbol: $^{40}_{19}\text{K}$. The bottom number can be left off ($^{40}\text{K}$) because the symbol already tells you the atomic number.

**Worked example 2:** Write potassium-40 in nuclear notation and count its particles (K, atomic number 19). The mass number is the number after the dash, 40. Put 40 on top and 19 on the bottom: $^{40}_{19}\text{K}$. p⁺ = 19. n⁰ = 40 − 19 = 21. e⁻ = 19 (neutral).

**Average atomic mass** is the decimal number on the periodic table. It is a weighted average of all the element's isotopes, so it is **closest to the mass number of the most common isotope**. Round it when no mass number is given.

**Worked example 3:** Magnesium (atomic number 12) has an average atomic mass of 24.305. Round to 24, so the most common isotope is magnesium-24, or $^{24}_{12}\text{Mg}$. n⁰ = 24 − 12 = 12.

**Stability.** Our notes say a nucleus is most stable when the numbers of p⁺ and n⁰ are the same, and an unstable nucleus comes from too many or too few neutrons.

**Watch out for:** writing the atomic number on top, putting the number of neutrons in the hyphen name instead of the mass number, thinking a new top number makes a new element (only a new bottom number, the protons, does that), thinking isotopes have different protons, and mixing up the whole-number mass number with the decimal average atomic mass.

checks.prompt: Iron (Fe) has atomic number 26. Which is the correct nuclear notation for iron-56?
checks.explanation: The mass number, 56, goes on top, and the atomic number, 26, goes on the bottom. Flipping them, or putting the neutrons (56 − 26 = 30) on top, is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Chlorine has two natural isotopes, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. Its average atomic mass is 35.45. Which isotope is more common?
checks.explanation: The average, 35.45, is much closer to 35 than to 37, so most chlorine atoms are chlorine-35. If the two were equally common, the average would be 36. Assuming the isotopes are equally common is the common mistake.

relearning.title: Do: flip the terms, then write an isotope step by step
relearning.description: Flashcards with a 3-question self-quiz, then a worked problem one step at a time.

cards.back: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
The name tag: the same in every isotope of an element. Change them and you get a new element.
Protons + neutrons. It is different in each isotope.
Element name, a dash, then the mass number: potassium-40 or C-12.
Mass number on top, atomic number on the bottom: $^{40}_{19}\text{K}$.
The decimal on the periodic table. Round it to find the mass number of the most common isotope.

checks.prompt: In $^{14}_{6}\text{C}$, what does the 14 stand for?
checks.explanation: The top number is the mass number (protons + neutrons). The bottom 6 is the atomic number, and the neutrons are 14 − 6 = 8. Reading the top number as the neutrons is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Which pair are isotopes of the same element?
checks.explanation: Oxygen-16 and oxygen-18 are both oxygen (same protons) with different mass numbers. Carbon-14 and nitrogen-14 share a mass number, but they are different elements, so they are not isotopes. Matching by mass number is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: If you change the top number of $^{12}_{6}\text{C}$ to 13, what do you get?
checks.explanation: The bottom number (6 protons) still says carbon. A new top number is a new mass number, so it is a new isotope, carbon-13. Thinking a new top number makes a new element is the common mistake.

body.problem: Sulfur (S) has atomic number 16. An isotope of sulfur has 18 neutrons. Write it in hyphen notation and in nuclear notation, and count its electrons.

steps.text: Protons: sulfur's atomic number is 16, so p⁺ = 16.
Hyphen notation uses the mass number: sulfur-34 (or S-34).
Nuclear notation: mass number on top, atomic number on the bottom: $^{34}_{16}\text{S}$.
Electrons: a neutral atom has e⁻ = p⁺ = 16.

checks.prompt: Your turn: an isotope of chlorine (atomic number 17) has 20 neutrons. What is its mass number? Type a number.
checks.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 17 + 20 = 37, so it is chlorine-37. Subtracting (20 − 17 = 3) or giving just the neutrons (20) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Your turn: which shows an atom with 6 protons and 7 neutrons?
checks.explanation: The mass number, 6 + 7 = 13, goes on top, and the atomic number, 6, goes on the bottom. Carbon-7 uses the neutrons instead of the mass number, and the last choice has the numbers flipped. Those are the two common mistakes.
